label: Few species reach range edges where climate alone kills them
claim: Only a few plants or animals extend their ranges so far that they are destroyed by the severity of climate alone; competition continues everywhere except at the extreme limits of life.
quote: we have reason to believe that only a few plants or animals range so far, that they are destroyed by the rigour of the climate alone.
section: The relation of organism to organism the most important of all relations
scope: geographic range limits of plants and animals

label: Natural selection preserves favourable and destroys injurious variations
claim: Because more individuals are born than can survive, individuals with any advantage, however slight, have the best chance of surviving and reproducing, while injurious variations are eliminated; this preservation of favourable and rejection of injurious variations is natural selection.
quote: This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection.
section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
scope: all organisms in nature

label: Neutral variations escape selection and remain fluctuating
claim: Variations that are neither useful nor harmful are not acted on by natural selection and stay variable, which may explain the variability of so-called polymorphic species.
quote: Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element, as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic.
section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
scope: characters of all organisms, especially polymorphic species

label: No native biota is so well adapted that it cannot be improved
claim: No country's native inhabitants are so perfectly adapted that none could be improved, as shown by introduced species having established firmly in every country.
quote: No country can be named in which all the native inhabitants are now so perfectly adapted to each other and to the physical conditions under which they live, that none of them could anyhow be improved; for in all countries, the natives have been so far conquered by naturalised productions, that they have allowed foreigners to take firm possession of the land.
section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
scope: native biotas of all countries and regions

label: Protective colours matching backgrounds are maintained by selection
claim: Seemingly trivial characters such as colour can be shaped by natural selection; colours that match the background, as in green leaf-eating insects and heather-coloured grouse, protect their bearers from predators that hunt by sight.
quote: When we see leaf-eating insects green, and bark-feeders mottled-grey; the alpine ptarmigan white in winter, the red-grouse the colour of heather, and the black-grouse that of peaty earth, we must believe that these tints are of service to these birds and insects in preserving them from danger.
section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
scope: animals preyed on by visually hunting predators

label: Natural selection can modify organisms at any age
claim: Because variations arising at a particular life stage tend to be inherited at the same stage, natural selection can modify organisms at any age, for instance adapting larvae independently of adults.
quote: natural selection will be enabled to act on and modify organic beings at any age, by the accumulation of profitable variations at that age, and by their inheritance at a corresponding age.
section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
scope: all organisms, especially those with distinct life stages such as insects with larvae

label: Males of polygamous species fight most and carry special weapons
claim: Fighting between males for females is perhaps most severe in polygamous animals, and the males of such species are the most often equipped with special weapons.
quote: The war is, perhaps, severest between the males of polygamous animals, and these seem oftenest provided with special weapons.
section: Sexual Selection
scope: animals with male-male competition for mates, especially mammals and birds

label: Female choice over many generations can produce male ornaments
claim: Female birds, by choosing the most melodious or beautiful males over thousands of generations, can produce a marked change in male song or plumage.
quote: I can see no good reason to doubt that female birds, by selecting, during thousands of generations, the most melodious or beautiful males, according to their standard of beauty, might produce a marked effect.
section: Sexual Selection
scope: birds, especially species with male display

label: Sex differences in species with shared habits are mainly sexually selected
claim: When males and females of a species share the same general habits of life but differ in structure, colour or ornament, those differences were mainly caused by sexual selection, although not all such differences are.
quote: Thus it is, as I believe, that when the males and females of any animal have the same general habits of life, but differ in structure, colour, or ornament, such differences have been mainly caused by sexual selection
section: Sexual Selection
scope: sexually dimorphic animals

label: Flowers and their insect visitors become mutually adapted
claim: A flower and a bee can slowly become modified and adapted to each other, at the same time or one after the other, by the continued preservation of individuals with mutually favourable slight differences in structure.
quote: Thus I can understand how a flower and a bee might slowly become, either simultaneously or one after the other, modified and adapted in the most perfect manner to each other, by the continued preservation of individuals presenting mutual and slightly favourable deviations of structure.
section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
scope: flowering plants and their insect pollinators

label: Natural selection works only by accumulating very small modifications
claim: Natural selection acts only by preserving and accumulating very small inherited modifications, each profitable to its bearer, and so excludes continued creation of new organisms or large sudden changes of structure.
quote: Natural selection can act only by the preservation and accumulation of infinitesimally small inherited modifications, each profitable to the preserved being
section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
scope: all organisms

label: Crossing increases vigour; close interbreeding decreases it
claim: In animals and plants, crosses between different varieties or between different strains of the same variety give vigour and fertility to the offspring, while close interbreeding reduces vigour and fertility.
quote: a cross between different varieties, or between individuals of the same variety but of another strain, gives vigour and fertility to the offspring; and on the other hand, that _close_ interbreeding diminishes vigour and fertility
section: On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species
scope: animals and plants, wild and domestic

label: No organism self-fertilises indefinitely; occasional crosses are needed
claim: It is a general law of nature that no organism fertilises itself for an unlimited number of generations; an occasional cross with another individual, perhaps at long intervals, is indispensable, even in hermaphrodites.
quote: it is a general law of nature (utterly ignorant though we be of the meaning of the law) that no organic being self-fertilises itself for an eternity of generations; but that a cross with another individual is occasionally—perhaps at very long intervals—indispensable.
section: On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species
scope: all plants and animals, especially hermaphrodites

label: Trees more often have separate sexes than other plants
claim: Trees, across all plant orders, have separate male and female flowers more often than other plants do, which helps pollen move between trees (though Hooker reported the rule fails in Australia).
quote: That trees belonging to all Orders have their sexes more often separated than other plants, I find to be the case in this country
section: On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species
scope: flowering plants, comparing trees with non-woody plants

label: Large populations favour natural selection by supplying more variations
claim: A large number of individuals favours natural selection because it gives a better chance for profitable variations to arise within a given period, compensating for lower variability in each individual.
quote: A large number of individuals, by giving a better chance for the appearance within any given period of profitable variations, will compensate for a lesser amount of variability in each individual, and is, I believe, an extremely important element of success.
section: Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals
scope: all species undergoing natural selection

label: Large areas produce more, faster-forming and wider-spreading new species
claim: Although small isolated areas can favour new species, modification is generally faster on large areas, and forms produced there, having beaten many competitors, spread most widely and give rise to the most new varieties and species.
quote: Finally, I conclude that, although small isolated areas probably have been in some respects highly favourable for the production of new species, yet that the course of modification will generally have been more rapid on large areas; and what is more important, that the new forms produced on large areas, which already have been victorious over many competitors, will be those that will spread most widely
section: Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals
scope: terrestrial species in continents versus islands and small regions

label: Freshwater biotas evolve and go extinct more slowly, keeping relict forms
claim: Because all freshwater basins together form a small area, competition among freshwater organisms has been less severe, so new forms have arisen more slowly and old forms have been exterminated more slowly there, which is why fresh water holds ancient and anomalous forms.
quote: All fresh-water basins, taken together, make a small area compared with that of the sea or of the land; and, consequently, the competition between fresh-water productions will have been less severe than elsewhere; new forms will have been more slowly formed, and old forms more slowly exterminated.
section: Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals
scope: freshwater organisms, compared with marine and terrestrial ones

label: Natural selection acts slowly, intermittently and on few species at a time
claim: Natural selection always acts very slowly, often only at long intervals of time, and generally on only a very few of the inhabitants of a region at the same time.
quote: On the other hand, I do believe that natural selection will always act very slowly, often only at long intervals of time, and generally on only a very few of the inhabitants of the same region at the same time.
section: Slow action
scope: all organisms within a region over geological time

label: Favoured forms make less favoured forms rare, and rarity precedes extinction
claim: Because every area is already fully stocked, as a favoured form increases in number the less favoured forms decrease and become rare, and rarity precedes extinction.
quote: it follows that as each selected and favoured form increases in number, so will the less favoured forms decrease and become rare. Rarity, as geology tells us, is the precursor to extinction.
section: Extinction caused by Natural Selection
scope: species in fully occupied areas, over ecological and geological time

label: New forms press hardest on and tend to exterminate their nearest relatives
claim: Because the most closely related forms compete most severely, each new variety or species, while forming, presses hardest on its nearest relatives and tends to exterminate them.
quote: Consequently, each new variety or species, during the progress of its formation, will generally press hardest on its nearest kindred, and tend to exterminate them.
section: Extinction caused by Natural Selection
scope: varieties and species, wild and domesticated

label: Divergence of character maximises the life an area supports
claim: The greatest amount of life can be supported in an area by great diversification of structure among its inhabitants.
quote: The truth of the principle, that the greatest amount of life can be supported by great diversification of structure, is seen under many natural circumstances.
section: Divergence of Character, related to the diversity of inhabitants of any small area, and to naturalisation
scope: local communities of plants and animals

label: The closest-competing neighbours tend to belong to different genera and orders
claim: Where organisms compete most closely, as on a small patch of ground, the advantages of diversification mean that the coexisting inhabitants generally belong to different genera and orders.
quote: where they come into the closest competition with each other, the advantages of diversification of structure, with the accompanying differences of habit and constitution, determine that the inhabitants, which thus jostle each other most closely, shall, as a general rule, belong to what we call different genera and orders.
section: Divergence of Character, related to the diversity of inhabitants of any small area, and to naturalisation
scope: small-area communities, e.g. turf plots, islets, small ponds

label: Naturalised floras add proportionally more new genera than new species
claim: Floras gain far more new genera than new species from naturalised plants, relative to the native numbers of genera and species, so naturalised plants tend to differ from the natives at the genus level.
quote: floras gain by naturalisation, proportionally with the number of the native genera and species, far more in new genera than in new species.
section: Divergence of Character, related to the diversity of inhabitants of any small area, and to naturalisation
scope: naturalised plants in regional floras

label: Intermediate forms and parent species tend to go extinct
claim: In a fully stocked country, improved descendants of a species tend to supplant their predecessors, so the intermediate forms between earlier and later states, and the original parent species itself, generally tend to become extinct.
quote: Hence all the intermediate forms between the earlier and later states, that is between the less and more improved state of a species, as well as the original parent-species itself, will generally tend to become extinct.
section: Action of Natural Selection, through Divergence of Character and Extinction, on the descendants from a common parent
scope: lineages of species descended from a common parent

label: Extinct species are often intermediate between living groups
claim: Extinct species, though generally in the same orders, families or genera as living ones, are often somewhat intermediate in character between existing groups, because they lived when the branching lines of descent had diverged less.
quote: the diagram throws light on the affinities of extinct beings, which, though generally belonging to the same orders, or families, or genera, with those now living, yet are often, in some degree, intermediate in character between existing groups
section: Action of Natural Selection, through Divergence of Character and Extinction, on the descendants from a common parent
scope: fossil and living species of all groups

label: Differences between varieties grow into differences between species and genera
claim: Through natural selection and divergence of character, the small differences between varieties of a species steadily increase until they equal the larger differences between species of the same genus, or even between genera.
quote: Thus the small differences distinguishing varieties of the same species, will steadily tend to increase till they come to equal the greater differences between species of the same genus, or even of distinct genera.
section: Summary
scope: varieties, species and genera of all organisms

label: Very few species of past periods have living descendants
claim: Like a tree in which only a few early twigs grew into surviving branches, very few of the species that lived in long-past geological periods now have living modified descendants, and many whole orders, families and genera have died out entirely.
quote: Of the many twigs which flourished when the tree was a mere bush, only two or three, now grown into great branches, yet survive and bear all the other branches; so with the species which lived during long-past geological periods, very few now have living and modified descendants.
section: Summary
scope: all lineages over geological time

label: Variability is induced by changed conditions acting on the reproductive system
claim: Deviations of structure arise in some way from the conditions of life to which parents and their ancestors have been exposed over several generations, acting chiefly by disturbing the reproductive system; hence variability is greater under domestication or cultivation than in nature.
quote: But the much greater variability, as well as the greater frequency of monstrosities, under domestication or cultivation, than under nature, leads me to believe that deviations of structure are in some way due to the nature of the conditions of life, to which the parents and their more remote ancestors have been exposed during several generations.
section: Effects of external conditions.
scope: plants and animals, domesticated and wild

label: Direct effects of climate and food on organisms are small
claim: The direct effect of differences in climate, food and similar conditions on an organism's structure is very small in animals and perhaps somewhat larger in plants, and cannot account for the complex co-adaptations between organisms.
quote: How much direct effect difference of climate, food, etc., produces on any being is extremely doubtful. My impression is, that the effect is extremely small in the case of animals, but perhaps rather more in that of plants.
section: Effects of external conditions.
scope: plants and animals in nature

label: Flightlessness of birds on predator-free oceanic islands is caused by disuse
claim: The nearly wingless condition of several birds living on oceanic islands that lack beasts of prey has been caused by disuse of the wings.
quote: I believe that the nearly wingless condition of several birds, which now inhabit or have lately inhabited several oceanic islands, tenanted by no beast of prey, has been caused by disuse.
section: Use and disuse, combined with natural selection; organs of flight and of vision.
scope: birds of oceanic islands

label: Wingless Madeira beetles result mainly from selection against being blown to sea
claim: The high proportion of flightless beetles on windswept islands such as Madeira is mainly due to natural selection favouring individuals that fly least and so avoid being blown out to sea, probably combined with disuse.
quote: these several considerations have made me believe that the wingless condition of so many Madeira beetles is mainly due to the action of natural selection, but combined probably with disuse.
section: Use and disuse, combined with natural selection; organs of flight and of vision.
scope: insects of oceanic islands, especially ground-living beetles

label: Blindness in cave animals results from disuse
claim: Because useless eyes are unlikely to be harmful in total darkness, the loss of eyes in most cave-dwelling animals is due to disuse alone rather than to natural selection.
quote: As it is difficult to imagine that eyes, though useless, could be in any way injurious to animals living in darkness, I attribute their loss wholly to disuse.
section: Use and disuse, combined with natural selection; organs of flight and of vision.
scope: cave-dwelling animals

label: Cave animals are related to surface fauna of their own continent
claim: Blind cave animals of America should be most closely allied to other inhabitants of America, and those of Europe to inhabitants of Europe, rather than the cave faunas of the two continents being specially similar to each other.
quote: Notwithstanding such modifications, we might expect still to see in the cave-animals of America, affinities to the other inhabitants of that continent, and in those of Europe, to the inhabitants of the European continent.
section: Use and disuse, combined with natural selection; organs of flight and of vision.
scope: cave faunas of North America and Europe

label: Species ranges are limited by competition as much as by climate
claim: Species in nature are limited in their geographic ranges by competition with other organisms at least as much as, or more than, by adaptation to particular climates.
quote: We have reason to believe that species in a state of nature are limited in their ranges by the competition of other organic beings quite as much as, or more than, by adaptation to particular climates.
section: Acclimatisation.
scope: plants and animals in nature

label: Homologous parts tend to vary together
claim: Parts of the body that are homologous and alike early in embryonic development, such as left and right sides or fore and hind limbs, tend to vary in a correlated way.
quote: The several parts of the body which are homologous, and which, at an early embryonic period, are alike, seem liable to vary in an allied manner
section: Correlation of growth.
scope: animals and plants with serially or bilaterally homologous parts

label: Taxonomically important characters may be useless products of correlated growth
claim: Structural differences that systematists treat as highly important, such as differences between outer and inner seeds of Umbelliferae, may arise entirely from unknown laws of correlated growth without being of any use to the species.
quote: Hence we see that modifications of structure, viewed by systematists as of high value, may be wholly due to unknown laws of correlated growth, and without being, as far as we can see, of the slightest service to the species.
section: Correlation of growth.
scope: plants and animals; characters used in classification

label: Natural selection reduces superfluous parts without compensatory enlargement
claim: Natural selection will in the long run reduce any part of the organisation once it becomes superfluous, saving nutriment, without necessarily causing another part to enlarge; and it can enlarge an organ without requiring reduction of an adjoining part.
quote: Thus, as I believe, natural selection will always succeed in the long run in reducing and saving every part of the organisation, as soon as it is rendered superfluous, without by any means causing some other part to be largely developed in a corresponding degree.
section: Compensation and economy of growth.
scope: all organisms, e.g. parasitic cirripedes losing the carapace

label: Parts repeated many times in an individual are variable in number
claim: When a part or organ is repeated many times in one individual, such as snake vertebrae or stamens of polyandrous flowers, its number is variable, whereas parts present in small numbers are constant in number.
quote: when any part or organ is repeated many times in the structure of the same individual (as the vertebræ in snakes, and the stamens in polyandrous flowers) the number is variable; whereas the number of the same part or organ, when it occurs in lesser numbers, is constant.
section: Multiple, rudimentary, and lowly organised structures variable.
scope: plants and animals with serially repeated parts

label: Parts unusually developed relative to congeners are highly variable
claim: A part developed to an extraordinary degree or in an extraordinary manner in one species, compared with the same part in closely allied species, tends to be highly variable within that species; the rule does not apply when the unusual part is shared by a whole group.
quote: _A part developed in any species in an extraordinary degree or manner, in comparison with the same part in allied species, tends to be highly variable_.
section: Parts developed in an unusual manner are highly variable: specific characters more variable than generic: secondary sexual characters variable.
scope: animals, especially birds, cirripedes and secondary sexual characters; Darwin could not confirm it for plants

label: Specific characters are more variable than generic characters
claim: Characters that distinguish species within a genus are more variable within species than characters shared by all species of the genus, because the former have varied since the species branched from a common progenitor.
quote: It is notorious that specific characters are more variable than generic.
section: Parts developed in an unusual manner are highly variable: specific characters more variable than generic: secondary sexual characters variable.
scope: species within genera of plants and animals

label: Congeners differ more in secondary sexual characters than in other parts
claim: Secondary sexual characters are highly variable, and species of the same group differ from one another more in their secondary sexual characters than in other parts of their organisation.
quote: species of the same group differ from each other more widely in their secondary sexual characters, than in other parts of their organisation
section: Parts developed in an unusual manner are highly variable: specific characters more variable than generic: secondary sexual characters variable.
scope: sexually dimorphic animals, e.g. gallinaceous birds

label: Long-lost characters reappear through a tendency transmitted each generation
claim: When a character lost in a breed reappears after many generations, the cause is a tendency to produce that character transmitted in every generation which at last prevails under favourable conditions, not a sudden resemblance to a distant ancestor.
quote: When a character which has been lost in a breed, reappears after a great number of generations, the most probable hypothesis is, not that the offspring suddenly takes after an ancestor some hundred generations distant, but that in each successive generation there has been a tendency to reproduce the character in question, which at last, under unknown favourable conditions, gains an ascendancy.
section: Reversions to long-lost characters.
scope: domestic breeds and wild species

label: Horse, ass, hemionus, quagga and zebra descend from a striped common ancestor
claim: The domestic horse, ass, hemionus, quagga and zebra are descended from a common ancestor that was striped like a zebra, which explains the occasional appearance of stripes in horses, asses and their hybrids.
quote: For myself, I venture confidently to look back thousands on thousands of generations, and I see an animal striped like a zebra, but perhaps otherwise very differently constructed, the common parent of our domestic horse, whether or not it be descended from one or more wild stocks, of the ass, the hemionus, quagga, and zebra.
section: Reversions to long-lost characters.
scope: genus Equus

label: Related species with shared constitution produce analogous variations
claim: Species that inherit nearly the same constitution from a common parent and are exposed to similar influences tend to produce analogous variations, so that a variety of one species may resemble another species of the same genus.
quote: Species inheriting nearly the same constitution from a common parent and exposed to similar influences will naturally tend to present analogous variations
section: Species of the same genus vary in an analogous manner.
scope: species within a genus, domestic races and wild species

label: Formation of a new form exterminates its parent and transitional varieties
claim: Because each new form tends in a fully stocked country to supplant and exterminate its less improved parent and other competing forms, the parent and all transitional varieties are generally exterminated by the process that forms the new species.
quote: Hence, if we look at each species as descended from some other unknown form, both the parent and all the transitional varieties will generally have been exterminated by the very process of formation and perfection of the new form.
section: Absence or rarity of transitional varieties.
scope: all species in fully stocked regions

label: Zones of overlap between representative species are narrow
claim: Where closely allied or representative species replace each other over a continuous area, the neutral territory between them is generally narrow compared with the territory occupied by each, and species become somewhat abruptly rarer towards their range limits.
quote: Hence the neutral territory between two representative species is generally narrow in comparison with the territory proper to each.
section: Absence or rarity of transitional varieties.
scope: representative species on continents, mountains and sea depths

label: Intermediate varieties are numerically rarer than the forms they connect
claim: Where varieties intermediate between two other forms occur in nature, they are generally much rarer numerically than the forms they connect, because they inhabit narrower intermediate zones.
quote: generally when varieties intermediate between two other forms occur, they are much rarer numerically than the forms which they connect.
section: Absence or rarity of transitional varieties.
scope: varieties of plants and animals in nature

label: Common forms improve faster and supplant rare intermediate forms
claim: Forms existing in larger numbers have a better chance in any given period of presenting favourable variations for natural selection, so they are improved faster and supplant the less numerous intermediate varieties between them.
quote: For forms existing in larger numbers will always have a better chance, within any given period, of presenting further favourable variations for natural selection to seize on, than will the rarer forms which exist in lesser numbers.
section: Absence or rarity of transitional varieties.
scope: varieties and incipient species

label: Bat flight arose from an apparatus for gliding
claim: Bats were derived from gliding animals, and the wing membrane extending to the tail and hind legs in some bats is a trace of an apparatus originally built for gliding rather than flight.
quote: In bats which have the wing-membrane extended from the top of the shoulder to the tail, including the hind-legs, we perhaps see traces of an apparatus originally constructed for gliding through the air rather than for flight.
section: Transitions in habits of life.
scope: bats and gliding mammals

label: Habits can change without corresponding change of structure
claim: Species sometimes have habits that do not match their structure, such as upland geese with webbed feet that rarely enter water or ground-living woodpeckers, showing that habits can change before structure changes.
quote: In such cases, and many others could be given, habits have changed without a corresponding change of structure.
section: Species with habits widely different from those of their allies.
scope: birds and other animals
